title: How a Go type satisfies an interface

steps.n: The interface lists the methods a caller needs.
A type defines methods with matching names and signatures.
The compiler checks the type has every method, with no declaration needed.
The caller's function takes the interface, so it accepts any matching type.
A test passes a small fake type that has the same methods.
A missing method is reported as a compile error.
The user runs the tool with flags such as a timeout and a path.
The flag package parses values and prints usage for mistakes.
main calls a function that returns an error instead of exiting inside it.
main maps errors to exit codes in one place.
The process ends with a status that scripts can test.
Messages go to standard error so output stays clean.

title: How ARP finds a MAC address

steps.n: Host A looks for host B's MAC address in its ARP cache.
Nothing is cached, so A broadcasts who has this IP address.
The switch sends the broadcast to every port in the subnet.
Host B answers directly with its MAC address.
Host A stores the mapping for a short time.
The frame goes to host B's MAC address through the switch.
A private host sends a packet to a public server.
The gateway records the private address and port against a public port.
The source address is changed to the gateway's public address.
The server answers to the gateway's public address and port.
The gateway finds which private host owns that port.
The destination is changed to the private host and the packet is delivered.
A bind mount maps an existing host path into the container.
Changes inside and outside the container appear in both places.
A named volume is managed by Docker and mounted at a path.
Data lives in Docker's own area, independent of the container.
The volume remains with its data until it is removed explicitly.
Host paths bring host ownership and permissions into the container.

title: Scanning an image before it ships

steps.n: The pipeline builds the image from the Dockerfile.
The scanner compares installed packages with a database of known vulnerabilities.
The policy fails the build for critical flaws with an available fix.
The team updates the base image or package and rebuilds.
The clean image is pushed to the registry.
New flaws are published daily, so stored images are scanned again.
The pipeline deploys the build and runs tests automatically.
Results are attached to the run.
The pipeline pauses and notifies the approver with the change and test results.
The approver reviews and approves, and the decision is recorded.
The same artifact that was tested is deployed.
A health check confirms the release, and the pipeline reports success.

title: Rolling back by redeploying an artifact

steps.n: The pipeline deploys build 42 to production.
The monitor shows error rates rising after the release.
The on-call engineer starts the rollback job with the previous version number.
The pipeline retrieves the stored v41 artifact, not a rebuild.
v41 is deployed with the same process as any release.
Error rates return to normal and the team investigates v42 calmly.
The controller creates pod 0 first with a stable name.
Pod 0 gets its own volume claim that persists.
The controller waits for pod 0 to be Running and Ready.
Only after pod 0 is ready is pod 1 created.
Pod 1 receives a separate volume claim.
A failed pod returns with the same name and the same volume.
Power loss stops the kubelet heartbeats.
After the grace period the node is marked NotReady and tainted.
Pods on the node are removed from the API after their toleration expires.
The Deployment's ReplicaSet creates new pods to restore the count.
The scheduler assigns the new pods to healthy nodes.
Traffic goes to the new pods once they are ready.

title: Checking a change with helm diff

steps.n: The engineer updates values or the chart version.
The diff plugin reads the manifest of the current release.
The new chart and values are rendered locally.
Lines are shown for each changed object.
The engineer checks image tags, replicas and resources.
Only then does helm upgrade run, with the diff attached to the review.
helm repo update downloads the list of available chart versions.
helm search shows several versions of the chart.
The engineer chooses an exact version, not the latest.
The chart is pulled and its values and templates reviewed.
The release is installed with the pinned version and recorded.
New versions are adopted by a reviewed change.
The engineer chooses a workspace named staging.
Each workspace has its own state in the same backend.
Resources for staging are created from the same code.
A second workspace uses another state, easy to confuse with the first.
Many teams use separate configurations and backends for clearer boundaries and permissions.
The plan header shows which environment is targeted.
Terraform creates resources one by one.
The cloud rejects a request, for example due to a quota.
The state records the resources created before the error.
The engineer reads the message and fixes the cause, such as raising the quota.
The next apply continues from the saved state.
The plan shows only the remaining work and no duplicates.
A task updates the configuration file.
The file differs, so the task reports changed.
The task notifies the restart handler.
The play continues with later tasks.
The restart runs once, after the tasks that needed it.
On a second run nothing changes and the service is not touched.
The playbook run starts with an inventory plugin.
The plugin lists servers with their tags.
The cloud returns servers and metadata.
Hosts are grouped by tag such as web or db.
The play targets the web group and connects to those hosts.
New servers are included next run and deleted servers disappear.
The load balancer requests the health path from each target.
Target A returns 200 and stays in rotation.
Target B is probed in the same way on the same path.
Target B returns errors repeatedly.
After the threshold, target B receives no new traffic.
Requests go to target A while B is repaired and re-added.
Usage and cost data is collected daily by tag.
The service compares spend with the monthly budget.
Forecast spend passes 80 percent of the budget.
The team receives an alert naming the service and the tag.
They find idle large servers left running.
They remove the servers and add scheduled shutdown for test environments.
Every request increments total and error counters.
A query computes the good request ratio over 30 days.
The ratio is compared with the 99.9 percent objective.
The dashboard displays the error budget remaining.
A second panel shows how fast the budget is being used.
The team slows releases if the budget is nearly spent.
The gateway creates an ID and passes it in a header.
The service writes the ID in every log line.
The service also sends spans with the same ID to the tracing backend.
An engineer searches logs for the ID.
The trace view shows the same request and where it was slow.
Logs show the error and the trace shows the slow call that caused it.
Weekly peaks for CPU, memory and storage are collected.
A forecast projects when usage will reach 80 percent.
The plan adds a margin for failures and launches.
The purchase or scale-up is scheduled before the date, with lead time.
The forecast is compared with actual growth.
Differences change the plan, not only the numbers.
The outgoing engineer lists open issues, recent changes and risky tasks.
The notes are shared in the handoff meeting or channel.
The incoming engineer asks about anything unclear.
Together they check open alerts and silences.
The incoming engineer confirms ownership and the pager is switched.
The outgoing engineer remains available for a short overlap.
The change updates dependencies.
The pipeline lists direct and indirect dependencies.
Versions are matched against known vulnerability data.
A critical flaw with a fixed version is found.
The developer upgrades to the fixed version.
The scan is clean and the pull request can merge.
The operator creates version 2 while version 1 remains valid.
The database accepts both passwords for now.
Service A reloads the secret and starts using version 2.
Logs show all instances connected with the new password.
Version 1 is removed from the database.
The date and owner are recorded for the next rotation.
The client commits a transaction.
The change is appended to the write-ahead log and flushed.
Only after the log is safe is the commit confirmed.
The data files are updated in the background.
The server loses power before data files are written.
On restart the log is replayed so committed changes are restored.

title: Running out of connections
summary: Why a pool and a limit matter.

steps.n: More application instances start, each opening its own connections.
The database hits its maximum number of connections.
New requests fail with too many connections.
An alert fires on connection use above 80 percent.
A pooler shares a small number of server connections among many clients.
Each application gets a limit so the total stays under the cap.

title: Choosing a cheaper model for simple steps

steps.n: Real requests are labelled by difficulty.
Simple classification is run on the cheaper model.
The evaluation set shows the pass rate matches the larger model on this step.
Hard reasoning steps stay on the more capable model.
The router sends each step to the cheapest model that passes.
The evaluation runs again on every model or prompt change.
A nightly job gathers ten thousand summaries to produce.
The requests are sent as one batch with IDs.
The provider processes them within a time window at a lower price.
The job checks the batch status periodically.
Results are returned with the same IDs.
Each result is matched to its request and validated, and failures are retried.
The instructions say what to do with the document.
The document is placed inside tags marked as data.
The prompt contains instructions first, then the tagged document.
The model summarises the content and does not follow orders written inside it.
Tags help but do not replace limiting what the system can do.
The output is validated in code before anything uses it.
The saved cases are run through version A several times.
The same cases are run through version B.
Checks in code score format, facts and forbidden content.
Pass rates, cost and latency are compared per case type.
The better version is released gradually.
Failures become new cases for the future.

title: Loading a reference file on demand
summary: Only when a step needs it.

steps.n: The request matches the skill and the body loads.
The steps run; most requests never need the long reference.
A step says to read the rules file for invoices over a limit.
Claude reads the single file named by the step.
The rules are applied to the task.
Other requests never pay for the reference in context.
The author improves a description or step.
The saved tasks are run before and after.
Results show better quality and no new false triggers.
The change is merged with a changelog entry and a new version.
The team installs the new version from the repository.
A missed request is added to the test tasks for next time.
The user selects a runbook in the host's attachment menu.
The host asks the server to read the resource by its URI.
The server loads the runbook from the backend.
The text is returned as the resource contents.
The host adds it to the model's context for the conversation.
Large documents are summarised or limited to save context.
Each conversation gets a run ID and each call a step number.
The agent calls a tool with arguments.
The call, duration, result size and errors are stored with the run ID.
Later steps are logged in order.
An engineer opens the trace for a wrong answer.
They see the tool returned an empty result and the agent gave up.

title: Failure and recovery: a full disk stops a service
summary: Logs fill /var, writes fail, and the fix has two parts.

steps.n: The service writes a little log data each second and the filesystem has plenty of free space.
A debug flag left on triples the log volume and nobody notices for days.
The filesystem reaches one hundred percent and the next write returns no space left on device.
Requests start failing and the service logs an error about being unable to write its own state.
The operator runs df -h to find the full filesystem and du -xh to find the biggest directories.
lsof shows a deleted log file still held open, so deleting it freed no space until the process restarts.
Truncate the log, restart the service to release the file, and turn the debug flag off.
Logrotate with size limits and a disk usage alert at eighty percent keeps it from recurring.

title: Failure and recovery: the OOM killer ends the wrong process
summary: Memory runs out and the kernel picks a victim.

steps.n: The application keeps asking for more memory as a cache grows without a size limit.
Free memory and page cache are used up and swap, if any, fills.
The kernel scores processes and ends the one with the highest score, which is the large database process.
A process-restart alert fires and the operator sees the database vanished at the same moment.
dmesg or journalctl -k shows Out of memory: Killed process with the process name and its memory use.
The real culprit is the cache with no limit, not the database that was killed.
Cap the cache size, set a memory limit with systemd, and protect the database with a lower oom score.
Memory graphs stay flat, no new kill messages appear, and the database stays up for a full day.

title: Failure and recovery: a force push overwrites a teammate's work
summary: Lost commits are usually still recoverable.

steps.n: Two people work on the same branch and the remote has three commits from the teammate.
The developer rebases locally and runs a plain force push because the normal push was rejected.
The remote branch now points at the developer's history and the teammate's commits are no longer on it.
The teammate's next pull reports a diverged history and the commits seem to be gone.
The teammate's own clone still has the commits and git reflog lists them by position.
Create a branch at the lost commit with git branch rescue and push it so the work is safe.
The developer rebases onto the rescue branch and pushes again, without losing either set of changes.
Protect shared branches and use force-with-lease instead of a plain force push.

title: Failure and recovery: a secret reaches the repository
summary: Rotating the secret matters more than rewriting history.

steps.n: A developer commits a file that contains a real access key and pushes it to the shared repository.
A scheduled scanner finds a string that matches the key pattern in the latest commit.
The scanner opens a finding and the security team is told which key and which commit.
The key is revoked and a new one issued before anything else, because anyone who cloned has the old one.
The file is removed from all commits with a history rewrite tool and the repository is force pushed.
Everyone re-clones or resets, since old clones and forks still hold the secret.
The new key is read from a secret manager at runtime and the file now holds only a placeholder.
A pre-commit hook and a push check block the pattern before it reaches the remote.

title: Failure and recovery: an unset variable deletes the wrong path
summary: A tiny script bug becomes a large deletion.

steps.n: A cleanup script runs rm -rf with a variable named BUILD_DIR followed by a slash.
A typo means BUILD_DIR was never set, so the shell expands it to an empty string.
The command becomes rm -rf slash, and only the protection of the system saves the whole machine.
Files under directories the user owns are deleted before the command is stopped.
A reviewer asks why the script did not stop when the variable was empty.
Add set -u so unset variables are an error, and use the expansion that fails when the value is empty.
Check that the path starts with the expected directory and exists before any delete.
Restore from backup and add a dry run option that only prints what would be removed.

title: Failure and recovery: a half-written file is read by another job

steps.n: A job writes its report straight to the final file name over a few seconds.
A second job reads the same file in the middle of the write.
The reader gets half the lines and builds a wrong summary without any error.
Numbers in the summary do not match, and the file modified time is within the reader's run.
The writer creates a temporary file in the same directory and writes everything there.
A rename onto the final name is atomic, so the reader sees either the old file or the complete new one.
A trap removes the temp file if the script fails, so no stale partial files remain.
Re-running both jobs together always gives a complete report.
